questions.title: A true character of the nerve action potential
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of the action potential?

options.B: Is conducted slower in thin nerve fibers
options.C: Is produced by a sub-threshold stimulus
options.D: Requires no energy
options.E: Starts with repolarization caused by outward movement of Cl-

explanations.A: Incorrect. The action potential is an all-or-none event, not a graded one — once threshold is reached its amplitude is fixed and does not scale with stimulus strength.
explanations.B: Correct. Conduction velocity rises with fibre diameter, so thinner nerve fibres conduct action potentials more slowly than thicker ones of the same type. This is why the thin C fibres are the slowest-conducting class and the thick A fibres the fastest, and it is one of the three determinants of conduction velocity alongside myelination and temperature. A thin fibre offers more internal resistance to the local current that depolarises the next patch of membrane, so that current spreads a shorter distance ahead of the active zone per unit time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sub-threshold stimulus produces only a local, non-propagated response; an action potential requires an adequate, threshold-or-greater stimulus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Restoring the ionic gradients the action potential disturbs (via the Na+-K+ pump) does require ATP, even though the spike itself is driven by passive ion flow down existing gradients.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The action potential starts with depolarization driven by inward Na+ movement, not repolarization or outward Cl- movement.

questions.learning_objective: State that conduction velocity increases with nerve fibre diameter, so thinner fibres conduct more slowly.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Conduction Velocity and Fibre Diameter

questions.title: Site of maximum Na+ channel density in a myelinated neuron
questions.question: The number of Na+ channels per square micrometer of membrane in myelinated neurons is maximum at which one of the following sites?

options.B: Cell body
options.C: Dendritic zone
options.D: Initial segment
options.E: Node of Ranvier

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axon terminal is specialised for neurotransmitter release via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, not for the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cell body carries a relatively low density of voltage-gated Na+ channels compared with the nodes; it is mainly a site of integration, not regeneration of the spike.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dendrites are largely a receiving surface and carry few voltage-gated Na+ channels relative to the nodes of Ranvier.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The initial segment does carry a high Na+ channel density, since it is where the action potential is first generated, but the internodal membrane's own Na+ channel density is concentrated even further, at each node of Ranvier along the axon's length.
explanations.E: Correct. In a myelinated axon the internodal membrane is insulated by myelin, and it is only at the nodes of Ranvier that the membrane is exposed and richly supplied with voltage-gated Na+ channels. Because each successive action potential is only regenerated at a node, this concentrated channel density at the nodes is what makes saltatory conduction possible, letting the impulse jump from node to node instead of being regenerated continuously along the whole membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier in a myelinated axon.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Saltatory Conduction

questions.title: What increases nerve conduction velocity
questions.question: The velocity of conduction of action potentials along a nerve will be increased by which one of the following?

options.A: Decreasing the diameter of the nerve fiber
options.B: Lengthening the nerve fiber
options.C: Myelinating the nerve
options.D: Local anesthetics
options.E: Pressure on the axons

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decreasing fibre diameter slows conduction, since conduction velocity rises with diameter, not falls.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The length of the fiber does not, by itself, change the velocity at which an action potential is conducted along it.
explanations.C: Correct. Myelinating a nerve fibre insulates the internode and restricts the voltage-gated Na+ channels to the nodes of Ranvier, so the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes and jumps between them (saltatory conduction) rather than being regenerated at every adjacent patch of membrane. This raises conduction velocity by up to fifty-fold compared with an unmyelinated fibre of the same diameter, while also conserving the energy the Na+-K+ pump would otherwise spend restoring ionic gradients along the whole membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Local anesthetics decrease membrane permeability to Na+ and reduce excitability, which slows or blocks conduction rather than speeding it up.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pressure on a nerve trunk impairs or abolishes conduction (especially in the larger A fibers), it does not increase conduction velocity.

questions.learning_objective: State that myelinating a nerve fibre increases its conduction velocity, via saltatory conduction.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Saltatory Conduction

questions.title: Basis of saltatory conduction in myelinated axons
questions.question: Saltatory conduction in myelinated axons results from which one of the following?

options.A: Salt concentration is increased beneath the myelin segments
options.B: Capacitance is decreased at the nodes of Ranvier
options.C: Non-gated ion channels are present beneath the segments of myelin
options.D: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at nodes of Ranvier
options.E: Membrane resistance is decreased beneath the segments of myelin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction is not explained by any change in salt concentration beneath the myelin; the myelin segments act as an electrical insulator, not a site of altered ionic concentration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the internodal (myelinated) membrane's capacitance that is decreased by the insulating myelin sheath, not the capacitance at the nodes themselves — the nodes are where the exposed, low-resistance membrane and the Na+ channels are concentrated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The myelin-covered internode has very few functional ion channels exposed to the extracellular fluid; it is the insulated, low-conductance segment, the opposite of what this option describes.
explanations.D: Correct. In a myelinated axon the internode is insulated by myelin and depolarises passively, while voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at the exposed nodes of Ranvier. An action potential generated at one node acts as the stimulus for the next, so the impulse is regenerated only at the nodes and appears to jump between them, which is what raises conduction velocity so sharply in myelinated fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Membrane resistance is increased, not decreased, beneath the myelin segments — the myelin's insulating effect raises resistance to current leak across the internodal membrane, which is part of why current spreads passively and efficiently toward the next node.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that saltatory conduction results from voltage-gated Na+ channels being concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Saltatory Conduction

questions.title: Mechanism of action of local anesthetic drugs
questions.question: Local anesthetic drugs take effect by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Internal block of the axonal voltage-gated sodium channel
options.B: Inhibiting the action of acetylcholinesterase in the synapse
options.C: Internal block of axonal voltage-gated potassium channels
options.D: Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the synapse
options.E: Blocking neurotransmitter release from neuronal terminals

explanations.A: Correct. Local anesthetics act on the axon itself by entering the nerve fibre and blocking the voltage-gated Na+ channel from its internal (cytoplasmic) side. This decreases the membrane's permeability to Na+, so the membrane can no longer depolarise fast enough to reach the firing level, and the action potential — and with it, conduction — is abolished in the affected segment of nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase would prolong, not block, cholinergic transmission at a synapse; that is not how local anesthetics act on a nerve fibre.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Local anesthetics act on the voltage-gated Na+ channel, not the K+ channel, and they act from within the axon rather than blocking K+ conductance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors describes a neuromuscular- or ganglionic-blocking drug acting at a synapse, not the axonal mechanism of a local anesthetic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Local anesthetics block conduction along the axon itself; they do not act by blocking neurotransmitter release from a nerve terminal.

questions.learning_objective: State that local anesthetics act by an internal block of the axonal voltage-gated Na+ channel.

questions.title: A property of continuous conduction
questions.question: Which of the following is true of continuous conduction?

options.A: Occurs by jumping of charges from one node of Ranvier to another
options.B: Is relatively slow in unmyelinated nerve fibers
options.C: Occurs in the neuro-muscular junction
options.D: Occurs in myelinated nerve fibers
options.E: Velocity of conduction is fast (120 met/sec)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Jumping of charges from node to node describes saltatory conduction in myelinated fibers, which is the opposite of continuous conduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Continuous conduction is the mode of propagation in unmyelinated axons: the action potential regenerates at every adjacent patch of membrane via a local circuit of current rather than jumping between insulated segments. Because every patch of membrane must be depolarised in turn, and conduction speed is proportional only to the square root of the fibre's diameter (with no saltatory speed boost from myelin), this mode is relatively slow compared with saltatory conduction in a myelinated fibre of similar size.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The neuro-muscular junction is a chemical synapse, not a form of axonal conduction; continuous conduction refers to propagation along an unmyelinated axon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Continuous conduction occurs in unmyelinated, not myelinated, nerve fibers — myelinated fibers instead use saltatory conduction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A velocity around 120 m/sec is characteristic of the fastest myelinated (large A) fibers using saltatory conduction, not of unmyelinated fibers using continuous conduction, which are far slower.

questions.learning_objective: State that continuous conduction along unmyelinated fibers is relatively slow compared with saltatory conduction.

questions.title: Nerve fibre class that is typically all unmyelinated
questions.question: Which of the following nerve fibres are typically all unmyelinated?

options.B: Aδ fibers
options.C: B fibers
options.D: C fibers
options.E: Aβ fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aα fibers are large, myelinated somatic motor fibers, one of the fastest-conducting classes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aδ fibers are myelinated (though thinner than Aα and Aβ), carrying fast pain and temperature sensation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. B fibers are the myelinated preganglionic autonomic fibers, an intermediate class between A and C fibers.
explanations.D: Correct. C fibers are the thinnest class of nerve fibres, under 1 micrometre in diameter, conducting at only 0.5-2 m/sec, and they are unmyelinated, which is why they are the slowest of all the classes. They are exemplified by postganglionic autonomic fibers and by fibers carrying slow (dull, aching) pain sensation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Aβ fibers are myelinated somatic sensory fibers carrying touch and pressure sensation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C fibers as the unmyelinated class of peripheral nerve fibres.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Nerve Fibre Types (A, B, C)

questions.title: Effect of myelination on axon signal propagation
questions.question: What effect does myelination have on axons?

options.B: It slows the propagation of signals along them
options.C: It prevents cross talk between adjacent axons
options.D: It allows them to conduct signals significantly faster
options.E: It is responsible for regeneration of the nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myelination is not primarily a protective/structural coating in the sense of shielding the axon from injury; its physiological role tested here is on conduction speed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myelination speeds up, rather than slows, the propagation of the nerve signal, by restricting the regenerated action potential to the nodes of Ranvier.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While myelin does have some insulating effect between fibers, the effect being tested here is on conduction velocity, not on preventing cross-talk between adjacent axons.
explanations.D: Correct. Myelination allows an axon to conduct signals significantly faster, because it restricts the voltage-gated Na+ channels that regenerate the action potential to the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) instead of being regenerated at every adjacent patch of membrane as in continuous conduction. This raises conduction velocity up to fifty-fold compared with an unmyelinated fibre of similar diameter.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Myelination is not the mechanism of nerve regeneration; regeneration of a damaged peripheral nerve fibre is a separate, distinct physiological process.

questions.learning_objective: State that myelination allows axons to conduct signals significantly faster, via saltatory conduction.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Saltatory Conduction

questions.title: Speed of saltatory conduction
questions.question: Regarding saltatory conduction, which of the following is true?

options.B: May reach 120 m/sec
options.C: Occurs by jumping from one neuron to another
options.D: Decreases gradually with distance till it disappears
options.E: Occurs in post-ganglionic nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated fibers, where the insulated internode forces the action potential to be regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier; unmyelinated fibers instead conduct continuously.
explanations.B: Correct. Saltatory conduction is the fastest mode of nerve conduction, and in the largest, most heavily myelinated A-alpha fibers it can reach up to about 120 m/sec — the top of the A-fiber conduction-velocity range (20 to 120 m/sec). This speed comes from the impulse jumping between nodes of Ranvier rather than being regenerated at every point along the membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction is the jumping of the action potential from one node of Ranvier to the next along a single axon, not a jump from one neuron to another (that would describe synaptic transmission).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Because saltatory conduction is an actively regenerated, all-or-none process at each node, it does not decrease in amplitude or fade with distance; its amplitude stays constant along the length of the axon.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Post-ganglionic autonomic fibers are C fibers, which are unmyelinated and therefore use continuous, not saltatory, conduction.

questions.learning_objective: State that saltatory conduction in the largest A fibers can reach conduction velocities up to about 120 m/sec.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Nerve Fibre Types (A, B, C)

questions.title: Where saltatory conduction occurs
questions.question: Regarding saltatory conduction, which of the following is true?

options.B: Is fast in unmyelinated nerve fibers
options.C: Occurs by jumping from one neuron to another
options.D: Velocity of conduction is slow (0.5-2.0 meter/sec)
options.E: Decreases gradually with distance till it disappears

explanations.A: Correct. Saltatory conduction occurs specifically in myelinated nerve fibers, where the myelin sheath insulates the internode and forces the action potential to be regenerated only at the exposed nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse appears to jump between them along the axon. This node-to-node regeneration is what gives myelinated fibers their much higher conduction velocity compared with unmyelinated fibers of similar diameter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Unmyelinated fibers use continuous conduction, not saltatory conduction, and continuous conduction is relatively slow rather than fast.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction jumps between nodes of Ranvier along one axon, not from one neuron to another; that would instead describe synaptic transmission.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A conduction velocity of 0.5-2.0 m/sec is in the C-fiber (unmyelinated) range; saltatory conduction in myelinated fibers is much faster, reaching up to about 120 m/sec in the largest fibers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction is actively regenerated at each node, so its amplitude does not decrease or fade with distance along the axon.

questions.learning_objective: State that saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated nerve fibers.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Saltatory Conduction

questions.title: A defining feature of Type A nerve fibers
questions.question: Regarding Type A nerve fibers, which of the following is true?

options.B: They have a prolonged spike duration (2.0 msec)
options.C: They conduct impulses with slowed velocity (0.5-2 m/sec)
options.D: They include postganglionic fibers
options.E: They are very sensitive to local anesthetic drugs

explanations.A: Correct. Type A fibers are the largest class of peripheral nerve fibers, ranging from 2 to 20 micrometres in diameter, which — together with their myelination — gives them the fastest conduction velocities of the three fiber classes (20 to 120 m/sec). They are exemplified by somatic motor fibers, and further subdivide into alpha, beta, gamma and delta subtypes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type A fibers have the shortest spike duration of the three classes, about 0.5 msec; a prolonged 2.0 msec spike duration instead describes Type C fibers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A conduction velocity of only 0.5-2 m/sec describes the slow Type C fibers, not Type A fibers, which are the fastest-conducting class.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Postganglionic autonomic fibers are Type C fibers; Type A fibers instead include somatic motor and sensory fibers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the thin, slow Type C fibers that local anesthetics depress first; Type A fibers are relatively the least sensitive to local anesthetics.

questions.learning_objective: State that Type A fibers have the greatest diameter of the three nerve fibre classes.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Nerve Fibre Types (A, B, C)

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.19

questions.title: A defining feature of Type C nerve fibers
questions.question: Regarding Type C nerve fibers, which of the following is true?

options.B: They carry the highest-magnitude nerve impulse
options.C: They conduct impulses with the slowest velocity (0.5-2 m/sec)
options.D: They include somatic sensory and motor fibers
options.E: They are very sensitive to hypoxia

explanations.A: Incorrect. Type C fibers have the smallest diameter of the three classes, under 1 micrometre; Type A fibers have the greatest diameter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no distinct property of a 'highest-magnitude' impulse — action potentials are all-or-none events of comparable amplitude regardless of fiber class.
explanations.C: Correct. Type C fibers are the thinnest and slowest of the three fiber classes, conducting impulses at only 0.5-2 m/sec — far slower than Type A (20-120 m/sec) or Type B (5-15 m/sec) fibers. This is because Type C fibers are unmyelinated and use continuous rather than saltatory conduction, so each adjacent patch of membrane must be depolarised in turn rather than the impulse jumping between nodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Somatic sensory and motor fibers are Type A fibers; Type C fibers are instead exemplified by postganglionic autonomic fibers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Type B fibers are the class most susceptible to hypoxia, while Type C fibers are actually the least affected by it.

questions.learning_objective: State that Type C fibers conduct impulses at the slowest velocity of the three nerve fibre classes.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Nerve Fibre Types (A, B, C)

questions.title: Effect of local anesthetic drugs on nerve excitability
questions.question: Regarding the excitability of nerve fibers, which of the following is true?

options.B: Is decreased by increased temperature
options.C: Is increased by decreased Na+
options.D: Is decreased by decreased Ca++ ions
options.E: Is completely lost by local anesthetic drugs

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is not the tested direction of the temperature-excitability relationship in this source; the fact this question tests is that local anesthetics completely abolish nerve excitability, listed as option E.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Excitability is not described as decreased by increased temperature in this source's own tested fact; the correct fact tested here concerns local anesthetics abolishing excitability entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decreased extracellular Na+ shrinks the size of the action potential rather than increasing overall excitability; it is a decreased extracellular Ca2+ that raises membrane Na+ permeability and increases excitability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is an increased, not a decreased, extracellular Ca2+ that stabilises the membrane and lowers excitability.
explanations.E: Correct. Local anesthetics such as those used clinically act by decreasing the membrane's permeability to Na+, so strongly that the membrane can no longer depolarise fast enough to reach the firing level. Because no action potential can then be generated at all in the anesthetised segment, the nerve's excitability there is described as completely lost.

questions.learning_objective: State that local anesthetic drugs completely abolish nerve excitability.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Factors Affecting Excitability

questions.title: Identifying a nerve blocker
questions.question: Which of the following is a nerve blocker?

options.B: Increased Na+ ions
options.C: Slight pressure
options.D: Strong catelectrotonus
options.E: Decreased Ca2+ ions

explanations.A: Correct. Local anesthetic drugs act by markedly decreasing the membrane's permeability to Na+, which prevents the membrane from depolarising to the firing level. Because no action potential can then be generated, conduction along the nerve is blocked, which is why local anesthetics are classed as nerve blockers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased extracellular Na+ permeability raises, rather than blocks, excitability; it is a fall in Na+ availability or permeability that impairs conduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Only a strong (not slight) sustained pressure on a nerve trunk is capable of impairing conduction, and even then it affects the large A fibers first while sparing the C fibers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Catelectrotonus (the region under a cathode) is associated with increased, not blocked, excitability — it is anelectrotonus (under the anode) that is associated with decreased excitability.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A decreased extracellular Ca2+ raises membrane Na+ permeability and increases excitability rather than blocking the nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify local anesthesia as a nerve blocker acting by decreased Na+ permeability.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Factors Affecting Excitability

questions.title: Mechanism of local anesthetic drug action on membrane permeability
questions.question: Local anesthetic drugs act by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the synapse
options.B: Decreasing membrane permeability to potassium
options.C: Blocking neurotransmitter release from neuronal terminals
options.D: Decreasing membrane permeability to sodium
options.E: Inhibiting the action of acetylcholinesterase at the synapse

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors describes a neuromuscular- or ganglionic-blocking drug's synaptic mechanism, not the axonal mechanism of a local anesthetic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local anesthetics act on Na+, not K+, permeability; decreasing K+ permeability is not their mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Local anesthetics block conduction along the axon rather than acting at the nerve terminal to block neurotransmitter release.
explanations.D: Correct. Local anesthetics act by decreasing the membrane's permeability to Na+, entering the axon and blocking the voltage-gated Na+ channel from its internal side. With Na+ permeability reduced, the membrane can no longer depolarise fast enough to reach the firing level, so the action potential — and conduction along that segment of nerve — is abolished.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase would prolong, not block, transmission at a cholinergic synapse; it is not how a local anesthetic acts on the axon.

questions.learning_objective: State that local anesthetics act by decreasing membrane permeability to Na+.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Factors Affecting Excitability

questions.title: False statement about the nerve action potential (EXCEPT)
questions.question: In the action potential of the nerve, all the following are true EXCEPT:

options.A: The rapid repolarization is due to increased K+ permeability
options.B: The duration of the isoelectric interval (latent period) is inversely proportionate to the speed of conduction
options.C: Decreasing the external Na+ concentration reduces the size of the action potential
options.D: The absolute refractory period is the period from the firing level until repolarization is completed

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Rapid repolarization is indeed caused by increased K+ permeability, as the voltage-gated K+ channels open (later and more slowly than the Na+ channels) and carry K+ out of the cell, returning the membrane toward its resting level.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). The latent period is the time the impulse takes to travel from the stimulating to the recording electrode, so for a fixed distance a shorter latent period means faster conduction — the two are inversely related.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Decreasing the external Na+ concentration reduces the inward Na+ driving force during depolarization, which shrinks the size (amplitude) of the action potential.
explanations.D: Correct (i.e. this is the FALSE statement, the answer to the EXCEPT). The absolute refractory period runs from the firing level to only the early part of repolarization, not until repolarization is completed. It exists because the voltage-gated Na+ channels have all opened and then been rapidly inactivated, and it ends once enough of those channels have returned to their resting state to be available again — well before the membrane potential has fully returned to rest.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the absolute refractory period ends in the early part of repolarization, not once repolarization is complete.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Refractory Periods

questions.title: Effect of doubling extracellular K+ on the resting potential
questions.question: Regarding nerve excitability, which of the following is true?

options.A: Chronaxie means the intensity of the stimulus that produces a response
options.B: An anelectrotonic response decreases the membrane potential and increases nerve excitability
options.C: K+ is the least permeable cation through nerve membranes
options.D: The resting potential becomes less negative if the K+ concentration outside the nerve membrane is doubled

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronaxie is a duration, not an intensity — it is the time needed for a stimulus at twice rheobase intensity to excite the nerve; rheobase is the intensity term.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An anelectrotonic response (under the anode) hyperpolarises the membrane and decreases excitability; it is the catelectrotonic response (under the cathode) that depolarises the membrane and increases excitability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Resting membrane permeability to K+ is relatively high, which is why the resting membrane potential lies close to the K+ equilibrium potential; it is not the least permeable cation at rest.
explanations.D: Correct. The resting membrane potential depends heavily on the K+ concentration gradient across the membrane. Doubling the extracellular K+ concentration reduces the steepness of the outward K+ gradient the resting potential depends on, which depolarises the cell — making the resting potential less negative (closer to zero) — and this is the mechanism by which hyperkalaemia raises nerve and muscle excitability.

questions.learning_objective: State that doubling extracellular K+ concentration makes the resting membrane potential less negative.

questions.title: How increased K+ raises nerve fibre excitability
questions.question: Increased K+ ions increase the excitability of nerve fibers by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Producing depolarization, thus reducing action potential amplitude
options.B: Producing depolarization, thus activating voltage-gated Na+ channels
options.C: Producing depolarization through decreased K+ efflux
options.D: Inhibiting the activity of the Na+-K+ pump
options.E: Hyperpolarization of nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes an effect on action potential amplitude, not the mechanism by which raised extracellular K+ produces the initial depolarization that increases excitability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While depolarization toward threshold does bring the membrane closer to activating Na+ channels, the mechanism specifically asked for here is how the depolarization itself is produced by the raised K+, which is via reduced K+ efflux, not via direct Na+ channel activation.
explanations.C: Correct. Raising extracellular K+ concentration narrows the K+ concentration gradient across the membrane, so less K+ leaves the cell down its (now shallower) gradient — a decreased K+ efflux. Because the resting potential depends heavily on that outward K+ movement, reduced efflux depolarises the membrane, bringing it closer to threshold and thereby increasing excitability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased extracellular K+ is not described as acting by inhibiting the Na+-K+ pump; its effect on excitability is via the resting potential and K+ efflux.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Increased extracellular K+ depolarises (does not hyperpolarise) the nerve fibre, which is exactly why it raises rather than lowers excitability.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that increased extracellular K+ raises excitability by depolarising the membrane through decreased K+ efflux.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Factors Affecting Excitability

questions.title: Calculating conduction velocity from latent period and distance
questions.question: If the distance between a stimulating electrode and a recording electrode is 2 cm and the latent period is 1 millisecond, the conduction velocity of the axon is:

options.B: 50 meter/sec
options.C: 40 meter/sec
options.D: 20 meter/sec
options.E: This cannot be determined from the given information

explanations.A: Incorrect. 100 m/sec does not match the calculation for this distance and latent period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 50 m/sec does not match the calculation for this distance and latent period.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 40 m/sec does not match the calculation for this distance and latent period.
explanations.D: Correct. Conduction velocity is calculated as distance divided by the latent period, since the latent period is the time the impulse takes to travel from the stimulating electrode to the recording electrode. Here, 2 cm (0.02 m) divided by 1 millisecond (0.001 sec) gives 0.02 m / 0.001 sec = 20 meters/sec.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The conduction velocity can be determined directly from the given distance and latent period, using velocity = distance / time; the information given is sufficient.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate nerve conduction velocity from a given inter-electrode distance and latent period.

questions.title: Loss of movement without loss of pain under sustained nerve pressure
questions.question: A patient sitting for a prolonged time with deep pressure on a nerve trunk (e.g. sitting on the leg) loses movement in the limb but pain sensation is preserved. The best explanation is that:

options.A: A fibers are more susceptible to hypoxia than B fibers
options.B: A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
options.C: Nerve fibers carrying slow pain sensations are A fibers
options.D: C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
options.E: C fibers are somatic motor nerves carrying voluntary movements

explanations.A: Incorrect. This vignette is explained by differential sensitivity to pressure, not to hypoxia, and it is B fibers (not A fibers) that are most susceptible to hypoxia.
explanations.B: Correct. Sustained pressure on a nerve trunk preferentially abolishes conduction in the larger, thicker A fibers, while the thin C fibers remain relatively intact. Since A fibers carry somatic motor function (and fast, sharp pain/touch), their loss explains the paralysis, while the surviving C fibers — which carry slow, dull pain — explain why pain sensation is preserved.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Slow (dull, aching) pain sensation is carried by C fibers, not A fibers; A fibers instead carry fast, sharp pain, touch and motor function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the A fibers, not the C fibers, that are more sensitive to sustained pressure, which is exactly why movement (an A-fiber, motor function) is lost while pain (partly a C-fiber function) is preserved.
explanations.E: Incorrect. C fibers are postganglionic autonomic and slow-pain sensory fibers; somatic motor fibers carrying voluntary movement are A fibers, not C fibers.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the differential pressure-sensitivity of A versus C fibers to explain selective motor loss with preserved pain sensation under sustained nerve compression.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Nerve Conduction > Nerve Fibre Types (A, B, C)

questions.title: Functional role of the absolute refractory period
questions.question: Regarding the absolute refractory period, which of the following is true?

options.A: It limits the number of action potentials that can be produced and propagated along nerve fibers
options.B: It increases the velocity of conduction along the nerve fibers
options.C: It is the period of time when a strong stimulus can initiate a second action potential
options.D: It reduces the energy utilized by nerve fibers
options.E: None of the above

explanations.A: Correct. During the absolute refractory period no stimulus of any strength, however strong, can produce a second action potential, because all the voltage-gated Na+ channels have opened and then been inactivated. By imposing a minimum interval between successive action potentials, the absolute refractory period sets an upper limit on the number of action potentials a nerve fibre can produce and propagate per unit time.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The refractory period does not increase conduction velocity; it instead limits how frequently a fibre can fire, which is a separate property from the speed of any single impulse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is the definition of the relative, not the absolute, refractory period — during the absolute refractory period, no stimulus of any strength can produce a second action potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The refractory period is not described as an energy-saving mechanism; its role is functional (limiting firing frequency and enforcing one-way propagation), not metabolic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option A correctly describes a true function of the absolute refractory period, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the absolute refractory period limits the number of action potentials a nerve fibre can produce and propagate.

questions.title: Timing of peak K+ efflux relative to the spike
questions.question: During nerve cell excitation, the peak of K+ efflux occurs:

options.B: Before the peak of Na+ influx
options.C: Coincident with the peak of Na+ influx
options.D: After both the spike and the peak of Na+ influx
options.E: In the after-depolarization phase of the action potential

explanations.A: Incorrect. K+ efflux is not the event that precedes the spike; the spike (the sharp Na+-driven rise and fall) comes first, with K+ efflux following.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The voltage-gated K+ channels open later than the Na+ channels, not earlier, so peak K+ efflux comes after, not before, peak Na+ influx.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The two are not coincident — the K+ channels are deliberately slower to open than the Na+ channels, which is what separates depolarization from repolarization in time.
explanations.D: Correct. Two events end the spike: inactivation of the Na+ channels stops the Na+ influx, while the K+ channels — which open shortly after the Na+ channels, more slowly and stay open for longer — carry K+ out to complete repolarization. Because the K+ channels open later than the Na+ channels and remain open after the Na+ channels have already inactivated, the peak of K+ efflux occurs after both the spike itself and the peak of Na+ influx that produced it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Peak K+ efflux drives repolarization (and the subsequent hyperpolarization/after-potential), so it occurs before, not during, the after-depolarization/after-potential phase — it is the cause of that later phase, not simultaneous with it.

questions.learning_objective: State that the peak of K+ efflux occurs after both the spike and the peak of Na+ influx during repolarization.

questions.title: A true statement about Type A fibers
questions.question: Regarding Type A fibers, which of the following is true?

options.A: They are very sensitive to local anesthetic drugs
options.B: They are very sensitive to O2 lack
options.C: They conduct impulses with slow velocity
options.D: They have the smallest diameter
options.E: They include somatic sensory and motor fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the thin, slow Type C fibers that local anesthetics depress first; Type A fibers are relatively resistant to local anesthetics compared with C fibers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type B fibers, not Type A, are the class most susceptible to hypoxia (O2 lack).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type A fibers conduct impulses with the fastest, not the slowest, velocity of the three fiber classes (20-120 m/sec).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Type A fibers have the greatest, not the smallest, diameter (2-20 micrometres); Type C fibers have the smallest diameter.
explanations.E: Correct. Type A fibers are exemplified by somatic motor fibers, and the class further subdivides into alpha, beta, gamma and delta subtypes, which together carry somatic sensory functions (touch, proprioception, fast pain) as well as somatic motor function. This mix of sensory and motor roles distinguishes Type A fibers from the autonomic Type B (preganglionic) and Type C (postganglionic) classes.

questions.learning_objective: State that Type A fibers include somatic sensory and motor fibers.
